en: The Abhidharma-sūtra of the Buddha, Chapter One: On the Characteristics of Renunciation, Volume Upper.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Chen and India.
Taking all the merit possessed by the sentient beings of one thousand asaṃkhyeya worlds, it constitutes one [unit] of the merit for attaining Buddhahood.
A single pore;
likewise, the merit of a single pore of a Buddha’s body, when multiplied by the number of all pores on the Tathāgata’s body, constitutes one secondary mark (*anuvyañjana*) of a Buddha.
Likewise, the merit of accomplishing the eighty secondary marks, increased a hundredfold, constitutes one primary mark (*lakṣaṇa*) upon the body of a Tathāgata.
The merit of the thirty-two marks thus accomplished is increased a thousandfold to form the single white tuft of hair (ūrṇā-kośa) between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows;
the merit of one thousand such tufts is further increased a hundredfold to form the Tathāgata’s cranial protuberance (uṣṇīṣa), the crown of which cannot be seen by any of the flying devas.
In this way, an inconceivable accumulation of pure merit accomplishes the Buddha-body.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is the most honored and supreme among devas and humans.
The Buddha said:
"The Buddhas of the past have said: 'O bhikṣus!
If you see the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination, you see the Dharma.
If you can see the Dharma, you then see the Buddha.'"
"What is the meaning of these words? Their meaning is this:
by means of these causes and conditions, to see the characteristics of the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination—whether they arise or do not arise—is itself the seeing of the Dharma."
If one can see that phenomena have both arising and non-arising, this is itself seeing the Buddha, for one follows after wisdom.
Furthermore, what are the names of the twelve links of dependent origination?
All Buddhas of the past have taught that the twelve links of dependent origination are explained by way of two meanings:
first, arising from causes; second, arising from conditions.
Furthermore, one should contemplate them through these two meanings.
First, external; second, internal.
Regarding the external conditions, they proceed from the meaning of "cause. Why is this?

All Buddhas of the past and future proclaim this in the same way: from the seed arises the sprout; from the sprout arises the leaf; from the leaf arises the node; from the node arises the stem; from the stem arises the trunk; from the trunk arise the branches; from the branches arise the buds; from the buds arises the flower; and from the flower arises the fruit.
If there is no seed, then a sprout will not arise; likewise, if there is no flower, then a fruit will not be produced.
Because there is a seed, a sprout can arise; likewise, because there is a flower, a fruit can be produced.
In this way, the seed does not say, "I can produce the sprout," nor does the sprout say, "I can produce myself"; thus all phenomena abide according to their true nature.
For this reason, external conditions should be viewed in terms of their causal significance; this is the contemplation of the meaning of causes.
What is the contemplation of the meaning of conditions?
It is like the nature of earth, the nature of water, the nature of fire, the nature of wind, and the nature of space.
As for the nature of earth, it can receive the seeds.
The nature of water can moisten the seeds.
The nature of fire can ripen the seeds.
The nature of wind can cause seeds to grow.
The nature of space can provide non-obstruction for seeds.

If these conditions are absent, seeds will not arise. Just as the nature of earth can receive seeds, the nature of water can moisten seeds, the nature of fire can ripen seeds, the nature of wind can cause seeds to grow, and the nature of space can provide non-obstruction for seeds, so too do seeds grow by depending upon the proper season; because the seeds grow, sprouts are produced.

The nature of the earth does not say, "I can receive the seed"; the nature of water does not say, "I can moisten the seed"; the nature of fire does not say, "I can ripen the seed"; the nature of space does not say, "I can provide non-obstruction for the seed"; and the seed itself does not think, "By means of these conditions, I am able to grow."
If separated from these conditions, the seed cannot produce a sprout.

Furthermore, this sprout is not self-created, nor created by another, nor created by Īśvara, nor born without cause; rather, the sprout arises from earth, water, fire, wind, space, the seed, and the season.
Furthermore, dependent origination should be examined through five aspects:
it is neither eternal nor annihilated; it does not involve a transmigration; because it relies on conditions, the fruit increases and expands; and it arises from that which is similar to itself.
Regarding the term "non-eternal": because this seed perishes, it is called non-eternal.
At the very moment the seed perishes, the sprout arises; because there is no obstruction, it is like the rising of a scale when one side descends, and thus it is called "not annihilated."
The seed and the sprout are not identical; therefore, it is said that there is no transference.
What was sown was small, yet the harvest of seeds is vast; therefore, it is said that the fruit increases and expands by virtue of conditions.
That various kinds [of seeds] produce corresponding fruits— that is, arising from what is similar—
is also not the case.
In this way, the production of fruit from a flower should be established according to reason.
In this way, external conditions should be examined in two ways.
Likewise, the meaning of internal conditions should also be examined in two ways:
first, from the perspective of causes; second, from the perspective of conditions.
Regarding the meaning of the internal conditions arising from causes: what is meant by "ignorance conditions volitional formations;

volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; and birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress"? It is through these that suffering increases in succession.
In this way, this mass of suffering accumulates and increases; thus, because of ignorance, volitional formations increase, and so on, up to: because of birth, old age and death increase.

If there were no ignorance, then volitional formations would not arise; if there were no birth, then there would be no aging and death. Thus, because there is ignorance, volitional formations increase; and because there is birth, aging and death increase.

That ignorance likewise does not think, "I am able to produce volitional formations," nor do the volitional formations think, "We have been produced by ignorance. This continues up to birth, which does not say, "I am able to produce old age and death," nor does old age and death say, "I have been produced by birth."
Thus, because there is ignorance (*avidyā*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) increase, and so on, up to: because there is birth (*jāti*), aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) increase.
What is called ignorance?
That which is referred to as "male" or "female" based upon the sixfold nature is what is termed ignorance.
What are the six kinds of nature?
They are the nature of earth, the nature of water, the nature of fire, the nature of wind, the nature of space, and the nature of consciousness.
As for the nature of earth, its characteristic is solidity; it is able to form the body and prevent the body from decaying.
The nature of water is also able to support, moisten, soften, and saturate.
The nature of fire is also able to support the flavors of what is drunk, chewed, and eaten, and is able to bring them to maturity.
The nature of wind is also able to support inhalation, exhalation, belching, panting, spitting, and so forth.
These are composed of the four great elements; the internal cavities are the element of space, continuing thus until they form name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
This is illustrated by the analogy of a bundle of reeds: the causal condition is the nature of consciousness (vijñāna).
The nature of that earth is not a self, not a sentient being, not a life-force, not male or female, and not oneself or another; this extends likewise even to the nature of consciousness.

Thus, because these six natures possess their conditions, there arise the notion of a sentient being, the notion of permanence, the notion of constancy, the notion of existence, the notion of a self, the notion of sensual desire, and the notion of "I."
Various types of ignorance such as these are called *avidyā* (ignorance).
Because this ignorance exists, one gives rise to attachment toward objects, gives rise to aversion, and gives rise to delusion.
When these [afflictions] of greed, hatred, and delusion arise based upon objects, they are termed "formations" (*saṃskāra*).
Because they involve the conceptual differentiation of phenomena, they are called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
From this consciousness, the four aggregates [of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness] further arise; this is "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
Based upon name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the sense-faculties arise; this is termed the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). From the gathering of these, contact (*sparśa*) arises;

from the sensing of contact, perception (*saṃjñā*); following perception, craving (*tṛṣṇā*); from the expansion of craving, grasping (*upādāna*); based upon grasping, there arises subsequent existence (*punarbhava*); because karma produces existence, there is becoming (*bhava*); with karma as the cause, there are the aggregates (*skandha*); from the arising of the aggregates, birth (*jāti*); from the maturation of the aggregates, old age (*jarā*); from the disintegration of the aggregates, death (*maraṇa*); from internal feverish distress, sorrow (*śoka*); from mental brooding, lamentation (*parideva*); and from the conjunction of body, consciousness, and the aggregates, suffering (*duḥkha*).

Because the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is a coming together, it is unsatisfactory; such categories as these are termed the secondary afflictions (upakleśa). Because of its meaning of obscuration, it is ignorance (avidyā); because of its meaning of formative activity, it is volitional formations (saṃskāra);

because of its meaning of discernment, it is consciousness (vijñāna); because of its meaning of firm establishment, it is name-and-form (nāmarūpa); because of its meaning of gateways of entry, it is the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana); because of its meaning of contact, it is contact (sparśa); because of its meaning of receiving, it is sensation (vedanā); because of its meaning of craving and grasping, it is clinging (upādāna); because of its meaning of producing renewed existence, it is becoming (bhava); because of its meaning of arising, it is birth (jāti); because of its meaning of maturing, it is old age (jarā); because of its meaning of disintegration, it is death (maraṇa); because of its meaning of feverish distress, it is sorrow (śoka); because of its meaning of mental reflection, it is lamentation (parideva); because of its meaning of afflicting the body, it is suffering (duḥkha).
Because its meaning is to afflict the mind, it is "unwholesome" (dausthulya); because its meaning is to be a portion of the secondary afflictions (upakleśa), it is "suffering" (duḥkha).

Thus, because it does not accord with the true nature of reality (dharmatā), it follows false practice; because it is characterized by non-knowing, it is "ignorance" (avidyā). From such ignorance, the three types of formations (saṃskāra) arise, which are wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.
Therefore, it is said that ignorance conditions volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

Because there are such volitional formations as these, there are wholesome consciousnesses, unwholesome consciousnesses, and neutral consciousnesses; for this reason, volitional formations condition consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Because there is wholesome [karma] following consciousness, it arises; from wholesome [karma], name-and-form (nāmarūpa) arises, and it likewise arises from unwholesome and neutral [karma]. Because consciousness is the condition, it is called "name-and-form."

Due to the growth of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), there arises the knowledge that performs its respective functions through the six gateways; because name-and-form is the condition for this, it is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Because of the six spheres of contact, the six types of contact arise; because these six sense bases are the condition for this, they are called contact (*sparśa*).

Because this contact arises, feeling arises; therefore, it is said that "feeling arises conditioned by contact. Because one experiences the flavors of various conditions with attachment, it is called "feeling" (*vedanā*).

Conditioned by feeling, it is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*): the state of being delighted and infatuated with pleasant forms, stained by their flavor, unable to relinquish them, and deeply craving them further—these are called craving.
Conditioned by craving, there is grasping; desiring further and seeking renewed existence, one performs actions of body, speech, and mind, which is called "conditioned by grasping, there is becoming.
Depending on karma, the aggregates arise; this is "conditioned by becoming, there is birth."
Because these aggregates arise, there is maturation and decay; therefore, it is said that birth is the condition for old age and death.
Thus, the twelve links of dependent origination arise, mutually depending upon one another and mutually giving rise to one another, revolving without beginning and without interruption.
Furthermore, because karma, consciousness, and so forth give rise to the twelve links of dependent origination in succession, four branches arise;
this follows the meaning of their causes. What are these four?
They are ignorance, craving, karma, and consciousness.

Regarding the existence of the seed of consciousness as the cause of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*): karma and the field serve as its causes, while ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) serve as the causes of affliction (*kleśa*).
In the absence of these karmas and afflictions, the seed of consciousness does not grow.

Thus, with this cause, the seeds of karmic consciousness take the field; because of ignorance, the seeds of consciousness are scattered, and because of craving, the seeds of consciousness are moistened.

Yet that ignorance does not give rise to the thought, "I am scattering the seeds of consciousness," nor does craving think, "I am moistening the seeds of consciousness," nor does karma think, "I serve as the field for consciousness," nor do the seeds of consciousness think, "I arise because of these conditions."

Furthermore, the seed of consciousness, dwelling within the field of karma, being moistened by craving and densely covered by ignorance, grows and produces the sprout of name-and-form within all the aggregates that are themselves unborn.
Thus, this sprout of name-and-form is not created by itself, nor created by another, nor created by both, nor created by Īśvara, nor is it born without cause.

Because of such karma and afflictions, the seed of consciousness grows to produce the sprout of name-and-form; yet it does not pass from this world to a future world, for it proceeds in accordance with the complete sufficiency of the causes and conditions of karmic fruit.

It is like looking at one's own face in a clear mirror: the face does not leave the body to enter the mirror, yet a similar image appears therein because the necessary causes and conditions are fully assembled.
In this way, this body perishes in one place and arises in another because the causal conditions of karma follow it and are fully present.

It is like the lunar disk, which appears here at a distance of thirty-two thousand yojanas; when one sees the form of the moon in water contained in a bowl, the moon does not fall from the sky to this place, nor does it come across the water, yet the image of the moon appears because the causal conditions are complete.
For example, if one holds fire in a sealed vessel, the fire burns without being extinguished, and the flame does not depart from the flame; it continues to burn according to its causes.

In the same way, the seeds of consciousness are produced by karma and afflictions; from these, they enter into a continuous succession and produce the sprout of name-and-form within phenomena that have no owner, because the necessary conditions are complete.

All the factors of existence (bhavāṅgas) are established according to reason; thus, regarding internal dependent origination (adhyātma-pratītyasamutpāda), it is so from the perspective of the meaning of cause, and it is so from the perspective of the meaning of condition—thus from the meaning of cause and thus from the meaning of condition.
As it is said in the Sūtras: "Such is dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), such is the arising of conditions.

Regarding these conditions, I shall now explain their sublime characteristics according to the Abhidharma: just as when men and women gather with sexual desire and the seasonal timing coincides, the seed of consciousness (vijñāna-bīja) continues within the woman’s womb and gives rise to the sprout of name-and-form (nāmarūpa); just as the eye depends on form, relies upon light to produce mental activity, and conditioned by these, visual consciousness arises.
In this way, visible form serves as the objective condition for visual consciousness, light serves as the precursor, and space serves as the non-obstruction;
thus does the mind arise. Without such conditions, consciousness does not arise.

If the eye-faculty is unimpaired, external objects such as visible forms serve as the objective conditions, light serves as the introductory condition, and space serves as the non-obstructive condition; when the mental faculty arises as its condition, it then functions in dependence upon the mind.
In this way, eye-consciousness arises from the conjunction of conditions consisting of the eye, forms, light, space, and the mental attention that serves as its condition.

Yet, the eye does not think, "I am acting as the support for eye-consciousness"; forms do not think, "I am acting as the object-condition for eye-consciousness"; the light of the environment does not think, "I am acting as the illumination for eye-consciousness"; space does not think, "I am acting as the non-obstruction for eye-consciousness"; and the mental attention that serves as the condition does not think, "I am acting as the mental attention-condition for eye-consciousness."
Visual consciousness also does not think,
"I am produced by depending on these conditions.
Rather, when these conditions exist, visual consciousness arises.
In this same manner, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness are explained extensively according to principle.
Abiding within clarity, the mental consciousness arises dependent upon the mind and mental objects (*dharmas*).
Thus it is explained extensively.
Thus, regarding the meaning of internal dependent origination from conditions, one should contemplate the meaning of internal dependent origination in this way.
One should examine it through five points:
it is neither eternal nor annihilated; there is no transmigration; because it relies on conditions, the fruit increases and expands; and it arises from that which is similar [to its cause].
This is also not the case.
Why? Because the aggregates at the moment of death perish, they are impermanent.
At that very moment, because the aggregates of death cease, other aggregates arise without interval or gap—like the rising of a scale when it has descended; therefore, it is not annihilation.
Because they are not identical, a superior mind arises from the initial mind; therefore, it is not a mere transmission.
Because one performs a small action and receives a great retribution, it is said that "by relying on conditions, the fruit increases and expands.
Because one receives a result that corresponds to the action performed, it is said that "it arises from similarity."
This is also not the case.

If, through the conditions of dependent origination, one knows that among the aggregates of the twelve links of dependent origination there is both arising and non-arising, then at that time, by employing a single consciousness, one can realize the Four Noble Truths as originally cultivated:
suffering is realized through wisdom, its origin through exertion, cessation through direct presence, and the path through contemplation.

Thus, for the true disciples who perceive the Four Noble Truths, this very perception is the perception of the Dharma; if they perceive the Dharma, they perceive the Buddha, thereby following the practice of wisdom.
What is the meaning of this?

Thus, through these causes and conditions, one perceives that the arising of the aggregates may be with birth or without birth; this is precisely the perception of the two truths, namely the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of Origination.
If one can perceive both of these causes and conditions, then by perceiving the first truth, one perceives the second truth—the Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path.
In this way, the true disciples who perceive the Four Noble Truths see all the Buddhas.
Because they follow after wisdom, a thought arises in their minds.
What is the analogy for this?

The reason for this is as follows: suppose there is a person who sees a skilled painter create a portrait with features and marks that are perfectly upright and handsome; they immediately give rise to the recognition:
"This painter is truly skilled at painting."
When these true disciples perceive the Four Noble Truths, they immediately give rise to this thought:
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is able to teach this Dharma for the sake of severing all suffering."

Thereupon, they give rise to incomparable faith in the Buddha; naturally and skillfully expounding this Dharma for the śrāvakas, they are well able to establish it in its profound and subtle mystery, thereby attaining firm faith in the Dharma.
Thereupon, this Abhidharma Sūtra was spontaneously and excellently expounded for the sake of severing all suffering.
If one can follow it accordingly, that is true compliance; thus, one gives rise to peerless faith toward the Saṃgha.

Having seen the true reality, one attains the pure and white category of precepts; one becomes free from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the clinging to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and all doubts are entirely abandoned.

Thus, when a true disciple has seen the Four Truths and possesses the four kinds of incomparable knowledge, they become free from the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and attain the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*); having realized the definitive Dharma and set out upon the path toward perfect enlightenment, they abide in the first fruit.
By attenuating lust, anger, and delusion, one becomes a Sakṛdāgāmin and abides in the second fruit.

By abandoning the five types of envelopments of the aggregates (*skandha-kaṣāya*) and the nine superior fetters (*ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*), and by diligently cultivating the path to exhaust all outflows and fetters, one becomes an Anāgāmin and abides in the third fruit.

Having completely abandoned sensual desire, conceit, self-exaltation, ignorance, and so forth, he attained the most excellent fourth fruit of the śramaṇa, became an arhat, and dwelt in nirvāṇa with remainder.
Thereafter, gradually abandoning all modes of existence, when the time comes for the body to perish and life to end, one immediately enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

By thus contemplating the characteristics of the arising of the aggregates of the body and thoroughly understanding the Four Noble Truths, the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat* are all realized and manifested.

In this way, through these various modes of contemplating the characteristics of the body's arising and awakening to the Four Noble Truths, one attains liberation; apart from this contemplation of the characteristics of the body's arising and the realization of the Four Noble Truths, the path to liberation cannot be attained.

If one desires to seek the path to liberation, seek the Four Noble Truths, seek incomparable faith, seek the attainment of the fruits of śrāmaṇya, or desires to enter nirvāṇa without remainder, one should diligently contemplate the characteristics of the arising of the aggregates (skandhas) according to the Abhidharma-sūtra.
The teaching of the Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment is thus. Now, next, we shall discuss the characteristics of the Vinaya.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, is reverently honored, respected, and made offerings to by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, and gandharvas. He has already attained excellent benefit and fulfilled his heart’s desires; he is free from all unwholesome dharmas and fully endowed with all wholesome dharmas. Without craving or grasping, he is detached from the notion of self. Having attained mastery over all modes of wisdom, he has severed the various realms of existence and the bonds of separation; being free from all afflictions, he is liberated and capable of liberating others. He turns the wheel of saṃsāra and the seeds of rebirth; he causes subsequent goodness to increase and prior goodness to manifest, enabling roots of virtue to attain liberation and extending his transformative teachings.
The Buddha appears in the world to adorn it and bring benefit to sentient beings.
The World-Honored One is their eye and their wisdom; he is their meaning and their Dharma, a great mass of the Dharma.

Toward these three kinds of sentient beings, the Buddha acts as a general to lead them, teaching and transforming them so that others may be led; he acts as a teacher so that others may become teachers.

He is a great caravan leader, able to know the paths and able to proclaim the excellent way; he is a great king of physicians, the unsurpassed wheel-turner, the most supreme among men, a hero who has received his final body;

he is a śramaṇa, a great śramaṇa who has attained the state of a śramaṇa; he is stainless, undefiled, luminous, pure, and all-seeing; he is able to bestow light and eyes, to remove darkness, to act as illumination and a guide, and to cross the ocean of birth and death; he brings peace to those who are not yet at peace; he is endowed with incomparable diligence and endowed with incomparable wisdom; he is a great hero, a great restrainer, one of great majesty, a great champion, a great deity, one of great power, and a great leader.
The World-Honored One is the foremost; the World-Honored One is the supreme.

The World-Honored One blows the Dharma conch, beats the Dharma drum, erects the Dharma banner, hoists the Dharma pennant, and kindles the Dharma lamp. He wards off the evil realms and reveals the auspicious realms; he removes the evils of the world and eliminates the perils of the world; he closes off the evil paths, opens the way to heaven, and shows the path of liberation.

By the power of supernormal knowledges he eliminates, and by the power of wisdom he extinguishes, all delusions in the minds of sentient beings; he rains down the rain of Dharma and manifests the four fearlessnesses.
Like the sun first rising and its radiance illuminating the world, he subdues all heterodox paths and establishes sentient beings in the heavenly realms and the fruit of liberation.
Having crossed over, he causes others to cross over; having been liberated, he liberates others; having attained peace, he brings peace to others; having attained nirvāṇa, he leads others to nirvāṇa.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling in the forest of Ṛṣipatana in the kingdom of Magadha.

King Bimbisāra of Magadha heard that the World-Honored One was accompanied by a great assembly of a thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were former practitioners of external paths who had exhausted their outflows, accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own benefit, exhausted the fetters of existence, and whose minds were liberated through right knowledge.

Having heard this, the king made grand preparations for his military forces with great majesty. By the power of the king, he mobilized twelve thousand chariots and eighteen thousand cavalry, and together with countless hundreds of thousands of brahmins and householders from the kingdom of Magadha, set out from Rājagṛha for the place where the Buddha was, desiring to see the Buddha and to make offerings to him.
When the carriage had reached its destination, the King immediately descended from it and proceeded on foot into the garden.

At that time, King Bimbisāra saw the Buddha from afar and immediately removed his fivefold regalia: namely, his precious robes and crown, his parasol, his jeweled sword, his precious ornamental fan, and his precious sandals.
At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and having paid respectful homage, thrice proclaimed his own name:
"O Virtuous One!..."
"I am King Bimbisāra of Magadha.
Thus he spoke three times.
The Buddha said:
"It is so. You are King Bimbisāra of Magadha.
He likewise repeated this three times.
“Great King!
Sit in your own seat.

Then King Bimbisāra of Magadha, having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew and sat to one side. The brahmins and householders of Magadha also gathered together in one place, and having likewise prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew and sat to one side.

At that time, the brahmins and householders of Magadha came to inquire after the Buddha’s well-being; having been comforted and exhorted by the Buddha in various ways, they withdrew and sat to one side.
Furthermore, the brahmins and householders of Magadha joined their palms, paid homage to the Buddha, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Furthermore, when the brahmins and householders of the kingdom of Magadha saw the Buddha from afar, they sat down in silence.
At that time, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa was seated nearby within this great assembly.
At that time, the brahmins and householders of the kingdom of Magadha each had this thought:
"Does this great śramaṇa study the Path under Uruvilvā Kāśyapa?"
"Is it that you, Uruvilvā, have come here to study the Way under this Great Śramaṇa?
Then the Buddha, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the brahmins and householders of the kingdom of Magadha, addressed Uruvilvā Kāśyapa with a verse, asking:
"You, Uruvilvā, for what reason and by what vision have you come here?"
"And having abandoned the worship of the sacrificial fire, why do you follow this path of study?
For such reasons as these, you ought to explain them to me:
why have you cast aside the fire that you formerly served?"
Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa replied: "Regarding food,
drink, and all such flavors— craving and indulging in these three types [of objects]—
I have deeply perceived the reasons for such faults."
"Therefore, having abandoned the practice of tending the sacrificial fire, your mind finds no peace.
The Buddha said:
"Your mind finds no peace even in the various flavors of food and drink."
"Why is it that your mind does not delight in the supreme path among humans and devas?
You should now answer me. Kāśyapa said:
"I have seen the extinction without remainder; the Path is supreme.
Toward the sensual pleasures of the world, my mind gives rise to no attachment.
There is no other distinct state; therefore, I do not follow any other teaching."
Therefore, I abandoned the service of fire and its offerings;
having completely eradicated my former crooked mind through this,
I attained liberation.
Following the stream of birth and death, they did not recognize the true and correct path;
now, for the first time, they behold the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
To the Great Assembly who take refuge, the World-Honored One is their general.
"I have now fully awakened to the true principles of reality, Gautama.
The Buddha said:
"Welcome to you who practice the Path; all that you have contemplated is indeed correct."
Having attained the most supreme [realization], you skillfully discern the characteristics of phenomena.
"Kāśyapa! You should resolve the doubts of the assembly."
Then the Elder Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa immediately entered into *samādhi*.

In accordance with the thought he had formed, he remained in the empty space of the eastern direction, manifesting the four dignified postures of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, while fire issued from within his body.

From the body of the Elder Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa issued various flames of light—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and the color of crystal—as he manifested miraculous transformations: the lower part of his body blazed with fire, while from the upper part of his body flowed clear, cool water.

Having thus displayed various supernatural transformations in the southern, western, and northern directions, they withdrew their manifestations, joined their palms toward the Buddha, paid homage, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha is our teacher; we are the Buddha’s disciples."
Thus he spoke three times:
"So it is, Kāśyapa! So it is, Kāśyapa!"
I am your teacher; you are my disciple.
Kāśyapa, sit upon your own seat; sit as you please.
Then the Elder Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa returned to his original seat and sat down.
At that time, the brahmins and householders of the kingdom of Magadha thought to themselves:
"It is certainly not the case that the Great Śramaṇa has learned the Way from Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa; rather, it is Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa who has learned the Way from the Great Śramaṇa."
Then the Buddha, the World-Honored One, addressed King Bimbisāra of Magadha:
"Great King!
Form also arises and ceases; this is what corresponds to arising and ceasing."
One should know, Great King, that consciousness, perception, feeling, and formations also arise and cease; they are associated with this arising and ceasing.
One should know, Great King, that form is a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing.
"Good son, having understood this matter, one knows that consciousness, perception, feeling, and formations are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing, Great King!
Good son, having understood this matter and having known this consciousness, Great King!"
"Noble son, one who knows form does not cling to it, does not grasp it, does not dwell upon it, and does not enter into it by reckoning consciousness, perception, feeling, or formations as 'self.
Noble son, having known this, one does not cling to them, does not grasp them, does not dwell upon them, and does not enter into them. Great King, noble son!"
Regarding form as the self,
one does not cling to it, does not grasp it, does not dwell upon it, and does not enter into it, thereby cultivating the mind of non-self.
I say that such a person attains immeasurable and boundless liberation from birth and death.
At that time, the brahmins and householders of the kingdom of Magadha each thought to themselves:
"If form is not the self, and if perception, feeling, volition, and consciousness are not the self, then who is it that constitutes the very essence of 'I,' 'person,' or 'sentient being'?"

If the agent and the action, the arouser and the aroused, the knower and the known, and such matters as these were truly non-arisen and non-existent, then in every place where the fruits of good and evil karma are produced, who would be the one to receive them? Who would cast off this aggregate (skandha), and who would take up the subsequent aggregate?
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the brahmins and householders of Magadha, addressed the bhikṣus:
"Those who claim 'self' are all foolish and ignorant, merely following the words of others; in reality, there is neither self nor anything belonging to a self."

Because suffering arises, there is arising; because suffering ceases, there is cessation. Because volitional formations arise, there is arising; because volitional formations cease, there is cessation. It is by depending on such causes and conditions that the bodily formations of sentient beings arise.
The Tathāgata knows the continuity and the arising and ceasing of sentient beings. Monks!

With the supreme eye, pure and surpassing that of humans, I see all: whether sentient beings arise with beautiful or ugly forms, whether superior or inferior, whether born in a good destination or a bad destination—I know all this as it truly is, according to their karmic laws.

These sentient beings, having committed evil deeds of body, having committed evil deeds of speech and mind, having slandered the virtuous and good, and being possessed of the causal conditions of the karma of false views, at the breaking up of the body after death, shall fall into the evil destinies and be born in the hells.

Furthermore, these sentient beings are endowed with wholesome karma of body, endowed with wholesome karma of speech and mind, and do not revile the virtuous; possessing right view, they act in accordance with the laws of karma associated with right view. By reason of these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they fall into a good destination and are reborn among the devas.
In this way, I know and see all this.
Yet I do not say: "This is the self," "this is a sentient being," "this is a life-force," or "this is a person."

This acts and this is capable of acting; this arises and this is capable of arising; there is that which can initiate and that which is initiated, as well as that which can know and that which is known. If such matters as these did not arise and did not exist, then in every place one would receive the fruits of the good and evil karma one has performed; yet, one abandons these aggregates and receives subsequent aggregates, with distinct dharmas depending upon one another.

Regarding their mutual dependence: because this dharma exists, that dharma arises—namely, with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, grasping; with grasping as condition, becoming; with becoming as condition, birth; and with birth as condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair arise. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering is produced.

With the non-existence of these, there is the cessation of these; through the cessation of this ignorance, volitional formations cease; through the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; through the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; through the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; through the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; through the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; through the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; through the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; through the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; through the cessation of existence, birth ceases; through the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease. In this way, this entire mass of great suffering ceases.
Thus it is, bhikṣus! All conditioned phenomena are suffering; nirvāṇa is peace and cessation.

Because of accumulation, suffering accumulates; because of cessation, suffering ceases. When the root is severed, it no longer continues; because it does not continue, there is cessation, and thus one reaches the ultimate end of suffering.
"Monks! What is called cessation?
It is the suffering that exists in this very place; because it ceases, there is stillness; because it is stilled, it is exhausted. This is the state of peace."
"If one is free from all afflictions and burdens, then craving is exhausted, desire is departed from, and there is the tranquility of Nirvana.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, again addressed Bimbisāra of the kingdom of Magadha:
"Great King!
“Is this form permanent or impermanent?
“It is impermanent,
World-Honored One.”
“Is this suffering permanent or impermanent?
“Suffering, World-Honored One, is impermanent.”
“Although these are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing, do the true disciples of the Śrāvakas conceive such thoughts as:
‘This follows me; this is mine; this is my substance; this is what belongs to me’?”
"This is not so, World-Honored One! "Great King!"
"What do you think?
Are consciousness, perception, feeling, and mental formations permanent or impermanent? "Impermanent."
“World-Honored One!
Are these sufferings permanent or impermanent?
“All sufferings are impermanent.”
“World-Honored One!
If this suffering is impermanent, then it is a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing.
Yet, the true disciples of the Śrāvakas conceive of it in this way:”
"Is it that 'this follows me,' 'this is mine,' 'this is my thing,' or 'this belongs to me'? "That is not so,
World-Honored One!"
"For these reasons, Great King!

Whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; superior or inferior; near or far—all of this is not 'I' or 'mine. In this way, one should contemplate it as it truly is with right wisdom."

Whether it be feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; superior or inferior; near or far—all these are not self, nor do they belong to a self. In this way, one should contemplate them as they truly are with right wisdom.

A true disciple, through such knowledge and vision, becomes weary of form; they likewise become weary of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Through weariness, they become dispassionate; through dispassion, they attain liberation. Because of liberation, they gain the wisdom that perceives:
"Birth has been exhausted, the outflows have been extinguished, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."
When these and other such teachings were spoken, King Bimbisāra of Magadha was freed from all defilements and cleansed of all impurities, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding the Dharma.
At that time, eighty thousand devas and immeasurable thousands of brahmins and householders from the kingdom of Magadha attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding the Dharma.

Then King Bimbisāra of Magadha saw the Dharma, attained the Dharma, understood the Dharma, and entered the profound Dharma; he transcended all longing and crossed over the net of doubt, no longer following the teachings of others nor having any further reliance on them, and he attained fearlessness within the Buddha’s teaching and Dharma.
Rising from his seat, he bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, paid homage, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I have already transcended; I have now indeed transcended."
I now take refuge in the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus; please remember me as an upāsaka.
From this day forth until the end of my life, I take refuge and maintain the purity of the precept of non-killing.
"I pray that the Blessed One will come to Rājagṛha; for as long as I live, I shall provide the Blessed One with offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites.
I pray that the Blessed One, together with the community of bhikṣus, will accept my invitation."
When King Bimbisāra of Magadha had thus made his invitation, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, remained silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted the invitation by remaining silent, King Bimbisāra of Magadha bowed his head to the Buddha’s feet in salutation, took his leave, and withdrew.
At that time, the World-Honored One set out toward Rājagṛha; having traveled by stages, he arrived at Rājagṛha and stayed in the Bamboo Grove where Kalandaka resided.
At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a śramaṇa named Sañjayin, who had not long since gone forth to teach. His followers had recently learned that their teacher had just passed away.
He had two companions leading a multitude of disciples:
one named Upatiṣya and the other named Kolita, both leading their respective groups of followers.
The two of them made this agreement together:
"Whichever of us first attains the supreme fruit of the Deathless (amṛta), we must certainly share it with the other.

Then, in the early morning, the Elder Aśvajit took his robe and bowl and entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms. At that time, the ascetic Upatiṣya was traveling through Rājagṛha on some minor business. From afar, the ascetic Upatiṣya saw the Elder Aśvajit; his heart was filled with joy as he gazed respectfully at him holding his robe and bowl. Having seen him, he thought to himself:
“Among those who have gone forth to study the Way within this city of Rājagṛha, I have never seen anyone with such dignified deportment.
I should now question this renunciant:
‘O mendicant, who is your teacher?’”
"For what purpose have you gone forth as a renunciant?
Under whose Dharma do you follow?
He stood by the road for the sake of making such inquiries.
When the Elder Aśvajit arrived, the ascetic Upatiṣya asked the Elder Aśvajit:
"O mendicant! Who is your teacher?"
"Under whom have you gone forth?
From whose Dharma do you follow? "Elder!"

There is a śramaṇa named Gautama, a son of the Śākyas, who has shaved off his hair and beard and donned dyed robes; possessing right faith, he has renounced worldly existence to leave the home life and train in the path to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
"This Blessed One is my teacher; I have gone forth under him, and I follow his Dharma.
"Venerable one, will you explain that Dharma to me?"

“Elder! I am still young in years, and my days of study are but recently begun; therefore, I have not yet been able to expound upon the profound and vast Dharma of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
"I shall now briefly explain a small portion of the meaning within the Dharma.
"I pray that you will explain it for me;
I require only the meaning, not the words."
Then the Elder Aśvajit spoke these verses:
“Whatever phenomena arise from a cause, The Tathāgata has declared their cause;
And that which brings about the cessation of such causes— This is the teaching of the Blessed One.”
When these and other such teachings were being spoken, the ascetic Upatiṣya was freed from defilement and stainless; he attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding the Dharma.

Having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, and understood the Dharma, the ascetic Upatiṣya entered into the profound Dharma, transcended all longing, and crossed over the net of doubt. No longer relying on others for faith and no longer following the instructions of another, he attained fearlessness within the Dharma of the Blessed One, the Buddha.
Rising from his seat, he bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and paid homage toward the elder Āśvajit, speaking these words again:

"Such profound dharmas as these, taught in the instructions of the World-Honored One—unshakable and free from sorrow or affliction—have never before been heard or seen throughout countless nayutas of kalpas."
“Where does the World-Honored One dwell now?
“He is right here in this city of Rājagṛha, at the Kalandaka Nivāpa in the Bamboo Grove.
When the ascetic Upatiṣya heard these words from the Elder Āśvajit, his heart was filled with joy; he prostrated himself at Āśvajit’s feet and withdrew.
Then the ascetic Upatiṣya went to visit the ascetic Kolita; seeing the ascetic Upatiṣya from afar, Kolita spoke these words:
"Your faculties are so serene and joyful; your facial complexion is pure, and the skin is radiant and white."
"Elder! Have you attained the Deathless? "It is so."
"Elder! Elder, please teach me the Dharma.
Then the ascetic Upatissa spoke this verse:
“Whatever phenomena arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause;
and for the cessation of such phenomena, the Blessed One has likewise taught the way. “Elder!”
"Please explain this to me once more.
"If a phenomenon arises from a cause, The Tathāgata has taught that cause;
The cessation of such causes— This is the instruction of the Blessed One."
When this Dharma had been taught, the ascetic Pāṭikāputra was freed from defilement and, being stainless, attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
Having seen the Dharma, having attained the Dharma, and having understood the Dharma, the ascetic Pāṭikāputra entered into the profound Dharma.

Having transcended the mind of hope and crossed over the net of all doubts, they no longer rely on other beliefs nor follow the teachings of others; within the Dharma of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they have already attained fearlessness.
Rising from his seat, he bared his right shoulder, joined his palms in homage toward Upatiṣya, and spoke these words again:
"Such profound dharmas as these, taught in the instruction of the World-Honored One—unshakable and free from sorrow—are things that for countless nayutas of kalpas I have never before heard or seen."
“Where does the Blessed One currently reside? [He replied:

“He is right here in Rājagṛha, at the Kalandaka-nivāpa in the Bamboo Grove. We should go together to visit the Blessed One and practice the holy life (brahmacarya) in his presence; we ought to go and see that assembly, for there too are wise men such as ourselves.”
Then Upatiṣya and Kolita, the two ascetics, addressed their brahmin disciples, saying:
"We wish to practice the holy life under the Buddha, the World-Honored One."
"What are you doing now?
They replied,
"Whatever knowledge we possess is entirely derived from our teacher's instruction."
"If the Teacher practices the holy life in accordance with the World-Honored One, we shall likewise follow the Teacher and go forth. "O Brahmins!
You should know that now is precisely the right time."
At that time, Upatiṣya and Kolita, each with their own retinue of two hundred and fifty people, departed from the city of Rājagṛha and went to where the World-Honored One was.
At that moment, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was preaching the Dharma for hundreds of thousands of countless sentient beings.
The World-Honored One saw from afar the two practitioners Upatiṣya and Kolita, each leading a retinue of two hundred and fifty followers.
Having seen them from a distance, he immediately addressed the bhikṣus:
"Bhikṣus, behold these two companions, Upatiṣya and Kolita and their followers, who are approaching this place at the head of their respective groups."
"So it is, World-Honored One!
These two shall become my foremost disciples in discipline and obedience."
"The first is foremost in supernatural powers; the second is foremost in wisdom.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the assembly who spoke a verse:
"Seeing these two men approaching, Upatiṣya and his companion,"
And when Kūṭadanta arrives, before he has reached this Bamboo Grove, the World-Honored One now makes this prophetic declaration:
"He possesses the boundless wisdom of the Buddhas;
his faculties transcend those of worldly men, and he is fully perfected in the pāramitās."
"Among those who have come from among the multitudes in this world, these two are the most supreme; they shall become the Great Disciples of the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One has already made a prophetic declaration:
one shall be foremost in supernormal powers, and the other foremost in wisdom."
Then Upatiṣya, Kolita, and the others came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. They addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We wish to go forth under the World-Honored One, receive full ordination, and become bhikṣus; we wish to practice the holy life under the World-Honored One.”
After Upatiṣya, Kolita, and the other practitioners of the way had gone forth under the teaching of the Dharma that is self-evident, received the precepts, and become bhikṣus,
those bhikṣus took up their robes and bowls at dawn and entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms.
At that time, the people of Rājagṛha saw the ascetic Sañjayin and his disciples leave the household life to receive the precepts. Having seen these bhikṣus, they rebuked them and spoke this verse:
“The Buddha has arrived at Rājagṛha, In the excellent kingdom of Magadha;
For what reason has he not fully converted The kinsmen of Sañjayin?”
At that time, the bhikṣus remained silent and offered no reply; they did not understand and lacked the eloquence to respond.

Having finished their alms-round in Rājagṛha in due order and concluded their meal, the bhikṣus returned to their quarters, laid aside their robes and bowls, and washed their feet. They then proceeded to where the Buddha was staying.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, they prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet and sat down to one side. Once seated, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This morning, we bhikṣus took up our robes and bowls and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food.”
At that time, the people of Rājagṛha, seeing that the ascetic Sañjayin and his followers had left the household life and received the precepts, collectively rebuked him by reciting these verses:
“The Buddha has arrived at Rājagṛha, In the supreme kingdom of Magadha;
Why has he not fully converted The followers of Sañjayin?”
At that time, the bhikṣus remained silent and offered no reply; they did not understand and lacked the eloquence to respond.
[The Buddha said: "If the people of Rājagṛha speak thus, you bhikṣus should answer them in this way:
'He whom the Great Hero leads across, The Tathāgata, by means of the True Dharma...'"
"Whosoever lacks wisdom would surely find it strange that wholesome dharmas gather in sentient beings.
When these words were spoken, the people of Rājagṛha immediately fell silent and offered no reply; they all lost their eloquence.
Then, at dawn, the bhikṣus again took up their robes and bowls and entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms.
At that time, the people of Rājagṛha, seeing the followers of the ascetic Sañjayin, rebuked them and spoke this verse:
“The Buddha has arrived in Rājagṛha, In the preeminent kingdom of Magadha.”
"Why has he not converted the entire retinue of Śāṇakavāsin?
At that time, another bhikṣu spoke this verse:
"The Great Hero is leading those to be delivered by means of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma."
"Virtuous dharmas gather in sentient beings; who that lacks wisdom would find this strange?
Having spoken thus, the people of Rājagṛha immediately fell silent, their eloquence lost.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, addressed the bhikṣus:
"Those who wear the dress and appearance of non-Buddhists should not be ordained and allowed to leave the household life.
The World-Honored One then established this precept:
"One who wears the dress and appearance of a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) may not be ordained as a renunciant.
At that time, there were bhikṣus who did not know how to ordain a non-Buddhist as a renunciant;
they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"For this reason, bhikṣus, you should seek further.
At that time, there was a non-Buddhist follower of the Vatsa lineage residing in the city of Rājagṛha.
Then the non-Buddhist follower Vatsīputra went to where the Blessed One was; having exchanged greetings with the Buddha and finished various forms of conversation, he withdrew to sit at one side.
Having sat down, the outsider of the Gautama clan addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now wish to ask the Gautama a few points; I pray that you will grant me permission to do so and explain them for me."
Having spoken these words, the World-Honored One remained silent.
A second and a third time they spoke thus.
Then the non-Buddhist of the Vatsa clan addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I now wish to ask the Great Virtuous Gautama a brief question; I only pray that you will grant me permission and explain it for me.
He spoke thus a second and a third time, but the World-Honored One remained silent.
Then the non-Buddhist ascetic of the Gokulika clan addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One Gautama, it has already been a long time since I arrived here this evening."
"I now ask concerning a small matter; I pray that you will grant me permission and explain it for my sake.
At that time, the Buddha thought to himself:

"This outsider of the Vātsīputrīya school has, throughout the long night, been without guile or crookedness, without deceit, and of a pure and straightforward nature. If he asks something, he already understands its meaning; he does not seek to trouble or disturb me."
"As with the esoteric meaning of the Abhidharma and the esoteric meaning of the Vinaya, one should explain it in detail when questioned.
Having known the thoughts in the mind of the Tīrthika Vatsiputriya, the Buddha said, "Vatsiputra, you may ask; ask whatever you desire."
“How is it, Gautama?
Do the wholesome and the unwholesome exist, or do they not? “Vatsa!”
“There is the wholesome and the unwholesome.
“Excellent, World-Honored One Gautama!
I pray that you will explain to me the wholesome and the unwholesome dharmas, so that I may recognize the wholesome and the unwholesome.”
“Vatsa! I shall explain to you in various ways the wholesome and the unwholesome;
however, I shall speak of them briefly.”
Vatsīputra, listen attentively.
Attachment to desire is unwholesome; freedom from attachment to desire is wholesome.
Hatred and delusion are unwholesome; freedom from hatred and delusion is wholesome.
Taking life is unwholesome; abstaining from taking life is wholesome.
Stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, and wrong view are unwholesome; right view is wholesome.
Vatsa! I have thus explained that these three types are wholesome and these three types are unwholesome.

If my disciple knows these unwholesome states as they truly are, and knows these three wholesome states and ten unwholesome states as they truly are; and regarding what remains beyond those ten unwholesome states, he knows the exhaustion of desire, the exhaustion of hatred, and the exhaustion of delusion; through the exhaustion of desire, hatred, and delusion, his outflows are exhausted, and by virtue of this exhaustion of outflows, he attains the state of being without outflows (*anāsrava*). His mind is liberated and he attains liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*); spontaneously seeing the Dharma and realizing the Dharma, he achieves its fulfillment:
"My births are exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further existence.

"Gautama, is there perhaps a single bhikṣu within this Dharma who has attained the exhaustion of all outflows, whose mind is liberated in the outflow-free Dharma, and who, as previously described, will not undergo further existence?"

“Vatsa! It is not one bhikṣu, nor two, nor three, nor five, nor a hundred; rather, countless bhikṣus like this have, within this Dharma, exhausted their outflows and attained the state of being without outflows, as previously described, no longer subject to future existence.”
“Gautama! Setting aside one bhikṣu for a moment,

is there perhaps even one bhikṣuṇī in this Dharma and Vinaya who has exhausted the outflows, attained the outflow-free mind, and achieved liberation as previously described, such that she will not undergo further existence?”

“Vatsa! It is not one bhikṣuṇī, nor two, nor three, nor five, nor a hundred—it is thus immeasurable bhikṣuṇīs who, within this Dharma, have exhausted their outflows and attained the outflow-free mind, achieving liberation as previously described, such that they shall not undergo further existence.”
“Gautama! Let us set aside the bhikṣuṇīs for now.
Is there perhaps some upāsaka who practices the holy life and, within this Dharma, transcends hope and transcends the net of doubt?”

“Vatsa! It is not just one lay follower, nor two, nor three, nor five, nor a hundred; rather, there are immeasurable lay followers who, within this Dharma, attain liberation from the fivefold fetters of attachment, are born by transformation, and attain parinirvāṇa right there, never to return again, for according to the nature of things, they do not return to this realm.”
“Gautama! Setting aside the bhikṣus, setting aside the bhikṣuṇīs, and setting aside the upāsakas who practice the holy life—
could there be any upāsikā who practices the holy life and has transcended hope and transcended the net of doubt?”

“Vatsa! It is not one, nor two, nor three, nor five, nor a hundred; rather, there are immeasurable upāsikās who, within this Dharma, attain liberation from the fivefold fetters of attachment, are born by transformation, and attain parinirvāṇa therein, never to return again, for by the nature of things they do not return to this realm.”
“Gautama! Let alone the bhikṣus;
let alone the bhikṣuṇīs; let alone the upāsakas practicing the holy life; let alone the upāsikās practicing the holy life.”
"Is there perhaps even one upāsaka who, while enjoying the fivefold sensual pleasures, has crossed over hope and crossed over the net of doubt within this Dharma? "Vatsa!

It is not just one upāsaka, nor two, nor three, nor five, nor a hundred; rather, there are immeasurable numbers who, within this Dharma—while possessing wives and children, bedding and dwellings, wearing fragrant flowers and garlands, wearing fine garments and various ointments, and keeping gold and jewels, and employing slaves, servants, and laborers—have been liberated from the three fetters, have attenuated lust, anger, and delusion, and have attained the stage of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), returning once more to this world to make an end of all suffering."

“Gautama! Let us set aside the bhikṣus; let us set aside the bhikṣuṇīs; let us set aside the upāsakas who practice the holy life; let us set aside the upāsikās who practice the holy life; and let us set aside the upāsakas who enjoy the fivefold pleasures of the senses.”
“Is there perhaps any female lay follower (*upāsikā*) who, while enjoying the pleasures of the five desires, has transcended hope and crossed over the net of doubt within this Dharma? “Vatsa!

It is not just one female lay follower, nor two, nor three, nor five, nor a hundred; rather, there are immeasurable numbers who, within this Dharma, raise their sons as previously described for servants and laborers, yet are liberated from the three fetters and turn back the stream of birth-and-death. They have attained the state of non-retrogression and will certainly realize perfect enlightenment. Having experienced these seven existences and seven births in the heavens, they shall again rely upon a human body to bring an end to all suffering.”

“If that were so, Gautama, if the Dharma of one who has attained perfect enlightenment were such that all bhikṣus, as well as bhikṣuṇīs practicing the holy life, upāsakas practicing the holy life, and upāsikās practicing the holy life—along with upāsakas who indulge in sensual pleasures and upāsikās who indulge in sensual pleasures—could attain it, then because the teaching of the World-Honored One Gautama is thus, it would not be fulfilled.”

For this reason, just as the bhikṣus who have attained perfect awakening through the Dharma established by Gautama all obtain [these fruits], so too do the bhikṣuṇīs, the upāsakas practicing celibacy, the upāsikās practicing celibacy, the upāsakas enjoying sensual pleasures, and the upāsikās enjoying sensual pleasures. Because it is thus, the teaching of Gautama is fulfilled in this way.
"Gautama!
I now wish to speak a parable.
"Vatsa! [The Buddha replied.]
"Now is precisely the right time.
"So it is, Gautama!"
Just as rain falling from the sky flows downward,

so too, World-Honored One Gautama, you instruct all men and women, boys and girls, whether old or young, to flow toward Nirvāṇa, to stream toward Nirvāṇa, to incline toward Nirvāṇa, and to follow the teaching of Nirvāṇa.
Having followed him, [he said]: "How wonderful, O Well-Awakened One! How wonderful, O Well-Spoken Dharma!

Gautama, if any wandering ascetic or practitioner of another path should come, seeking to go forth and receive full ordination as a bhikṣu according to this spontaneously arisen teaching of the Dharma, for how long must he dwell in dependence upon the bhikṣus?"

“Vatsa! If an outsider who has left the household life comes, seeking to leave the household life and receive full ordination as a bhikṣu according to the teaching of the natural Dharma, he should be made to wear the kāṣāya for four months under the supervision of a bhikṣu preceptor to test him, so that both sides may thoroughly investigate him.”
"I have already spoken thus.

"Gautama! If a renunciant from another sect comes seeking to go forth and receive full ordination as a bhikṣu according to the teaching of the Natural Dharma, he should be made to wear the saṃghāṭī robe for four months under the supervision of a bhikṣu preceptor to undergo a trial period."
I now wish not only for four months, but even for four years, to follow [the Teacher].

I now desire and delight in going forth from home under the teaching of the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) to receive full ordination and become a bhikṣu; I shall practice the holy life (brahmacarya) in reliance upon the World-Honored One Gautama.
“Vatsa! Have I not already explained those two points to you in full?
“You have indeed explained them, Gautama.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus!
Ordain the ascetic of the Vatsa clan, granting him the going-forth and the full precepts."

Once the ascetic of the Gotamīya clan had obtained the teaching of the natural Dharma, gone forth, and received full ordination (*upasampadā*), and after the Elder of the Gotamīya clan had likewise received full ordination and completed the half-month probationary period, he attained wisdom; he should train, he should contemplate, he should reach, and he should realize.
These wise ones have already seen, known, awakened to, and realized the True Dharma of the Blessed One.
At that time, the Venerable Ghoṣila had this thought:

"The wisdom I ought to train in—that which should be trained in, observed, attained, and awakened to—all such wisdom has been seen, known, awakened to, and realized by these wise ones as the True Dharma of the Blessed One."
"Now is precisely the right time for me to go to the place where the World-Honored One resides.

Thereupon, the Elder Ghoṣila went to the place where the World-Honored One was; having arrived at the World-Honored One's presence, he prostrated himself at the World-Honored One's feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Having stepped aside to one side, the Elder Ghoṭamukha addressed the Blessed One in this way:
"Blessed One!
Regarding wisdom, I should train in it, I should contemplate it, I should attain it, and I should realize it."
With all this wisdom, I have already seen, known, and realized the True Dharma of the Blessed One.
Excellent, Blessed One!
Please teach me the Dharma.
"May I draw near to non-negligence, and so forth, until I am as one who does not know that there is an afterlife.
For this reason, [he said]: "O calf!"
One should cultivate two dharmas: contemplation and extensive practice.
By cultivating these two dharmas—contemplation and extensive practice—one attains innate wisdom (*prakṛti-prajñā*).
Having awakened to all natures, one knows various natures and awakens to various natures; one knows immeasurable natures and awakens to immeasurable natures.
Vatsa! If a bhikṣu should think:
"How wonderful that I am free from all desires!"
"I am free from all evil and unwholesome states.
With the subsiding of directed thought and evaluation, he dwells in the first dhyāna, which is peaceful and blissful.
Through the cessation of directed thought and evaluation, with internal joy, he dwells in the second dhyāna, one-pointed, without directed thought or evaluation.

Being detached from joy, he dwells in equanimity; mindful and clearly aware, he experiences bodily bliss. Thus, he attains and abides in the third dhyāna, which is characterized by the noble truth of equanimity, mindfulness, and bliss.

Detached from pleasure and detached from pain, with the extinction of sorrow and joy, neither suffering nor happy, possessing equanimity and mindful purity, he dwells in the fourth dhyāna. [He likewise dwells in] loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
and in the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
How wonderful!

I have already abandoned the three fetters and attained the stage of Srotāpanna; having abandoned the three fetters, my lust, anger, and delusion have become attenuated, whereby I have become a Sakṛdāgāmin;
and by abandoning the five lower-tier fetters, I have become an Anāgāmin, accomplishing various supernormal powers.
With the faculty of the eye purified, the faculty of the ear purified, and the faculty of the mind purified, they return to their original state;
having escaped birth and death and exhausted all outflows, they are all endowed with such qualities and various supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-bala*):
they can manifest an infinite body from a single body, and can manifest a single body from an infinite body; they can create light and create darkness, and are fully possessed of these.
Observing various wisdoms, he passes through stones and walls; his body is free from obstruction and passes through the great earth as if it were empty space.
He can emerge from and submerge into the great earth as if in water;
he dwells in mid-air in the full lotus posture and travels like a bird in flight.

The sun and moon possess great majestic radiance, yet he can touch and grasp them with his hands; even ascending to the Brahma Heaven, he attains mastery through the supernormal power of *ṛddhi* regarding all that he aspires to within his own Dharma-gate.
"How wonderful it is that I, a bhikṣu, with the purified ear surpassing that of ordinary humans, hear two kinds of sounds:
those of devas and those of humans.
Whether near or far, whatever I direct my attention toward appears before me, provided there is aspiration within my own dharma-gate."
"How wonderful it is that I am a bhikṣu!
I know other beings; I know their aspirations, their deliberations, and whatever thoughts arise in their minds, knowing them all as they truly are."

In this way, he knows a mind with desire as it truly is; he knows a mind free from desire as it truly is, perceiving it as free from desire. Likewise, he knows a mind with desire and a mind free from desire; he knows a mind with aversion and a mind free from aversion, a mind with delusion and a mind free from delusion. He knows a mind that is concentrated and a mind that is distracted; a mind that is haughty and a mind that is not haughty; a calm mind and an extremely calm mind; a mind that is attentive and a mind that is inattentive; and a mind that is liberated and a mind that is unliberated, knowing each as it truly is.
According to where the mind is directed, one is able to obtain what is wished for, fulfilling all hopes regarding one's own dharma-gate.

How joyful it is that I am this bhikṣu, who through immeasurable kinds of analytical recollection knows past events: such as one birth, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, and thus immeasurable hundreds of thousands of births.
In this way, he fully recollects and knows the immeasurable number of past and future kalpas:

"In the past, there was a certain sentient being named so-and-so; at that time, I was named so-and-so, with such a lineage, such food and drink, such experiences of pleasure and pain, such longevity, such a duration of life, and such a limit to my lifespan."
"I died there and was reborn in such-and-such a place; having died there again, I am now born here.
Thus, according to their appearance and location, they recollect and know with various distinctions the events experienced in the past.
Whatever the mind inclines toward, this is attained according to its wish; whatever aspirations one has regarding one’s own dharma-gate, they are fulfilled.

How joyful am I, a bhikṣu! With the faculty of the eye purified, surpassing that of ordinary humans, I see beings at the time of death and the time of birth—whether their appearance is beautiful or ugly, whether they are increasing or decreasing, whether they are proceeding toward a good destination or an evil destination—and I know, as it truly is, how beings fare according to their respective deeds and karma.

These sentient beings are possessed of evil deeds of body, evil deeds of speech, and evil deeds of mind; they revile the virtuous and good, hold wrong views, and possess the causes and conditions for the habitual practice of the karma of wrong views.
Due to these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the evil realms and are born in hell.

Furthermore, there are other sentient beings who possess wholesome karma of body, possess wholesome karma of speech and mind, do not slander the noble and virtuous, and who, possessing right view, practice the dharmas that constitute the causes and conditions for right view.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they will proceed to a good destination and be reborn in the heavens.
Whatever their minds incline toward, they shall obtain as they wish, fulfilling all their aspirations within their own Dharma-gate.

"How wonderful it is that I am a bhikkhu who has exhausted all taints, whose mind has attained taintless liberation, and who, having attained liberation through wisdom, has fully realized the natural law:
'Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence hereafter.'"
According to the direction of one's mind, one is able to attain what is wished for;

regarding all that is hoped for within one’s own dharma-gate, the Dharma realized is certified by joy and bliss, and according to the direction of one's mind, one is able to attain what is wished for within one’s own dharma-gate.
"O bhikṣus! These two dharmas should be cultivated, observed, and extensively practiced.

Having cultivated these two dharmas—having cultivated, observed, and extensively practiced them—one achieves natural wisdom and natural awakening, becoming endowed with manifold natural wisdom, immeasurable natural wisdom, and immeasurable natural awakening."

When the Elder Ghoṣila had heard what the Buddha spoke, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; having prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, he took his leave of the Buddha and withdrew.
At that time, the Elder Ghoṣila had attained the most supreme and foremost Dharma; free from negligence and free from feverish distress, his mind attained mastery and dwelt in peace.

If a son of good family desires to do so, he shaves off his hair and beard, dons robes of a discolored hue, and with right faith abandons the conditioned to go forth into homelessness toward the unconditioned.
This unsurpassed holy life and pure dharma, having personally realized and fully attained the Dharma, [one knows]:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."
Having thus fully awakened, that elder attained the fruit of arhatship and his mind was liberated.
At that time, a great multitude of bhikṣus, seeking with diligence to see the World-Honored One and to make offerings to him, [set out].
At that time, the Elder Gopaka saw many bhikṣus and spoke to them again, saying:
