"We wish to go to where the World-Honored One is; we wish to see the World-Honored One and to make offerings to the World-Honored One."

"Please, Venerable One, convey my words to the World-Honored One, paying homage at his feet and inquiring after his health: whether he has little illness and little affliction, and whether he is light in movement, at ease, and living in comfort.
The Venerable Ghoṭamukha has spoken thus:
'I have established myself.'"
"Blessed One!
I have long practiced joy; it is not that I do not practice joy.
Thus, Blessed One, regarding the duties to be performed by a disciple as an offering to the Blessed One, I perform them with joy; it is not that I do not perform them with joy."
Then the bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was; having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, they prostrated at his feet and sat down to one side.
Once seated to one side, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

The Elder Gokulika prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and inquired after his health, asking whether he was free from illness and affliction, whether his daily life was light and easy, whether his strength was sufficient for his travels, and whether he lived in peace and security without hindrance.
The Elder Gokulika spoke thus:
"I have established it,
World-Honored One!"
"I have long practiced this,
World-Honored One!
It is joy, not the absence of joy."
"In this way, O Bhikṣus, that which is to be done by a disciple of the Blessed One—the making of offerings to the Blessed One—I have performed with joy, not without joy.
"O Bhikṣus! [he said.]
The devas have already told me of this matter; you shall speak of it after them.
Through his unsurpassed wisdom, the Tathāgata knows and sees that such a bhikṣu likewise possesses great supernormal power and great majesty.
Then, after the Blessed One had thus praised the Elder Ghoṭamukha, he spoke as follows:
“Monks, by not relying on an agent, one attains *sātisāra*.”

If non-Buddhist practitioners or Daoist priests come seeking ordination, and if a bhikṣu grants them the going forth even though he does not allow them to dwell together [with the Saṃgha], he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
How does one dwell together with non-Buddhists?
If a non-Buddhist comes seeking to go forth, they should immediately request a four-month period of probation from the Saṃgha.
They should pay homage to the assembly, saying:
"I, [Name], a member of a non-Buddhist sect, seeking the Dharma and teachings realized by the Tathāgata, request to go forth, receive full ordination, and become a bhikṣu.
I, [Name], a member of a non-Buddhist sect, now petition the Saṃgha for a four-month period of residence."
"I pray that the virtuous Saṃgha will grant me leave to dwell for four months out of compassion.
This should be said a second and a third time.
The *karmavācanā* master should then address the assembly:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This outsider named [Name] seeks the Dharma and teaching realized by the Tathāgata, and desires to go forth, receive full ordination, and become a bhikṣu."
This outsider, [Name], requests from the Saṃgha a stay for four months.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; if the Saṃgha so desires, it shall grant this outsider, [Name], a stay for four months.
The motion is thus made.
The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) should be performed as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This outsider, so-and-so, seeking the Dharma and teaching awakened by the Tathāgata, has gone forth and received full ordination as a bhikṣu.
This outsider, so-and-so, requests from the Saṃgha a four-month period of residence; if the Saṃgha grants this outsider, so-and-so, a four-month period of residence.
"Whichever elders consent to grant the four-month stay to this certain outsider, let them remain silent; whoever does not consent, let them speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*.
Thus is the second *karmavācanā*, thus is the third *karmavācanā*."
"The Saṃgha grants such-and-such a person a four-month period of residence.
The Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent; thus this matter is upheld.
Regarding that person's food and drink, if they perform services for the Saṃgha, they shall be given food from the portion allotted to the Saṃgha.
If one does not provide for the Sangha, one should say:
"You must seek food for yourself.
That non-Buddhist practitioner should then beg for food on their own.
The bhikṣus should, within a single day, pass before the followers of other paths three times and disparage them, speaking thus:

"The followers of other paths lack reverence and faith; the followers of other paths violate the precepts; the followers of other paths lack a sense of shame; the followers of other paths are fallen; the followers of other paths hold wrong views."
The Elder should speak as above.
At that time, he should further praise the fivefold virtues of the Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, Arhat, and so forth.
The non-Buddhist should say:
"It is so, Elder!"
"So it is, Elder!
It is true that the outsiders lack respect and faith, and so on, up to: it is true that the outsiders hold wrong views."
"May the Elder rescue me; may the Elder deliver me, out of compassion and pity.
Having lived together for four months and having been tested, and having gained the approval of the bhikṣus, he should be ordained, go forth, and receive full ordination.

If other non-Buddhists come in the guise of laypeople, they too should likewise live together [with the community] for a trial period before being permitted to go forth and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Even if there are non-Buddhists who understand the Dharma, they too should, as mentioned above, live together for a trial period before being permitted to go forth and receive full ordination.

If a follower of an external path has not undergone communal residence (*sāṃvāsika*) and the aforementioned trials, he shall not be ordained, allowed to go forth, or receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
If a bhikṣu ordains someone to go forth and receive full ordination without such trials, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, is reverently honored, respected, and made offerings to by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, and gandharvas.

He has already attained excellent benefit and fulfilled his heart’s desires; he is free from all unwholesome dharmas and is fully endowed with all wholesome dharmas. Without craving or grasping, he is free from the notion of self. Regarding all modes of wisdom, he has attained mastery; he has severed the various realms of existence and severed all separation. Free from all afflictions, he is liberated and capable of liberating others. He turns the wheel of saṃsāra and the seeds of birth and death; he causes all subsequent goodness to increase and prior goodness to manifest, enabling sentient beings to attain liberation through the extension of his teachings.
The Buddha appears in the world to adorn and bring great benefit to sentient beings; the World-Honored One is their eye and wisdom, their meaning and Dharma, and is this great mass of Dharma.
Among the three types of sentient beings, the Buddha acts as their general, leading, guiding, and transforming them so that others may be led;
he acts as their teacher, enabling others to become teachers.
He is a great caravan leader, capable of knowing the paths and able to proclaim the virtuous way;
he is a great king of physicians, the unsurpassed wheel-turner, the most excellent among men, a hero who has received his final body.

The Śramaṇa, the Great Śramaṇa, has attained the stainless, undefiled, luminous, and all-seeing state of a śramaṇa; he is able to bestow illumination and the eye, removing darkness, acting as light and as a guide across the ocean of birth and death. He brings peace to those who are not yet at peace; he is endowed with peerless diligence and peerless wisdom. He is the great hero, the great restrainer, the one of great majesty, the great champion, the great deity, the one of great power, and the great leader. The World-Honored One is the foremost; the World-Honored One is the supreme.

The World-Honored One blows the Dharma conch, beats the Dharma drum, erects the Dharma banner, hoists the Dharma pennant, and kindles the Dharma lamp; he blocks off the evil realms and points out the good realms, removes the evils of the world and the perils of the world, covers the evil paths, opens the way to the heavens, and reveals the path to liberation.

By the power of supernormal knowledges he removes, and by the power of wisdom he extinguishes, all delusions in the minds of sentient beings; he rains down the rain of Dharma and manifests the four fearlessnesses, like the rising sun whose radiance illuminates the world, subduing all heterodox paths and establishing sentient beings in the heavenly realms and the fruit of liberation.

Having crossed over, he helps others cross; having attained liberation, he helps others attain liberation; having found peace, he helps others find peace; having attained *nirvāṇa*, he helps others attain *nirvāṇa*.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there were certain bhikṣus who ordained others by the formula "Come, bhikṣu.

The Buddha said:
“A bhikṣu must not ordain others by saying ‘Come, O Bhikṣu’;
if he does so ordain them, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Thus the twenty *nidānas*, including the twenty prior causes and conditions, have been explained in detail.

The World-Honored One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

"How is it that these bhikṣus take the three refuges as their full ordination, yet their deportment and robes are all so disarrayed?

"If one who has the appearance and dress of a layperson receives full ordination, they incur a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was respectfully honored and served, until finally all unwholesome dharmas were extinguished in succession.

"How can these bhikṣus ordain and grant full admission to those with whom they have not shared the period of co-residence?"

Thus the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was reverently honored and served, until finally all unwholesome dharmas were extinguished in succession.
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a bhikṣu ordained a eunuch, granting him the full precepts.
Then, some bhikṣus of few desires criticized and marveled at this matter, saying:
“How is it that these bhikṣus have allowed eunuchs to go forth and receive full ordination?
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha,

"Are you able to act as the preceptor for [Name]?
The preceptor should reply:
"I am able."

This person, so-and-so, is appointed as the instructor for so-and-so.

"If the time for the Saṃgha has come, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen; let the Saṃgha authorize [Name] to act as the instructor for [Name], with [Name] as the preceptor (upādhyāya).
This is the formal motion (jñapti).
"Listen, son of good family!

"They are complete."

“‘I grant permission.

Within the body and upon the person of a man, there are such diseases as leprosy, carbuncles, white leprosy, scabies, sores, jaundice, emaciation, asthma, wasting, epilepsy, fever, blood-tumors, prolapse of the genitals, the coiling and knotting of tendons and veins, the accumulation of blood, fleshy growths, oral diseases, mouth-coating, heat in the mouth, heat in the body, heat in the abdomen, pain in the bones and joints, hiccups, vomiting, labored breathing, chills and fever, body aches, aches in the abdomen, and aches in the back; malaria occurring on the first, second, third, or fourth day; and various illnesses characterized by congealed pain, broken bones, and toothache.
"Are there no such diseases as these, nor any other diseases within your body?
He replied, "There are none."
"Have you already left the household life?
He replied, "No."
If he answers,
"I have already gone forth," one should ask as follows:
"Is your observance of the precepts free from any impairment or deficiency? He replied, "No."
"If your mind is weary and indolent, you may relinquish the precepts according to the Dharma.
[The teacher asks: "In the past, when you went forth, what was your name?
[The candidate] replies:

He replies:

Within the assembly, you shall also be questioned on these aforementioned matters; just as I have now questioned you, you must speak the truth when it is true and speak what is not true when it is not true."
"Stay here for a moment; we will call you when it is time to come.
The Preceptor then came into the midst of the assembly and said:

The assembly should all say:

I, [Name], request the Venerable Sangha to grant me full ordination, calling upon my preceptor by name, [Name], for the sake of a specific purpose."
May the virtuous Saṃgha grant me full ordination; may the virtuous Saṃgha accept me; may the virtuous Saṃgha take me in.
Out of compassion for me, out of compassion for me.
The second and third times were spoken in the same manner.

This person, [Name], seeks to receive full ordination from the preceptor [Name]."
This person, [Name], requests full ordination from the Venerable Sangha, with [Name] as preceptor.

"Are you a male? Are you already twenty years of age? Are your three robes and alms bowl complete?
"They are complete. "Do your parents still live?"

To each question, they replied:

Within the body of a man, there are such diseases as leprosy, carbuncles, white leprosy, scabies, sores, jaundice, emaciation, asthma, wasting, epilepsy, fever, blood abscesses, prolapse of the genitals, the coiling and knotting of tendons and veins, blood stagnation, fleshy growths, mouth-mucus, heat in the mouth, heat in the body, heat in the thighs, pain in the bones and joints, hiccups, vomiting, labored breathing, chills and fever, body aches, thigh pains, and back pains; there are fevers that recur every day, every two days, every three days, or every four days; and various combined ailments such as bone-breaking pain and toothache."
"Are there no such diseases as these, nor any other diseases within your body?
He replied, "There are none."
"Have you already left the household life?
He replied, "No."
If he answers,

"Is your observance of the precepts free from any impairment or deficiency? He replied, "No."
"Because of mental indolence, I have relinquished the precepts according to the Dharma.
[The teacher asks: "In the past, you once went forth;
what was your name? He replies:

"What is the name of your preceptor?
He replies:

Thereupon, one should make the formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This person, [Name], seeks to receive full ordination from the preceptor, [Name].
This person is a male, twenty years of age, possesses the three robes and an alms bowl, and declares himself to be pure and free from all obstacles to ordination.
This person, [Name], requests the Sangha of Venerable Ones for the conferral of full ordination, with [Name] as preceptor.
If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent; the Sangha shall confer full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as preceptor.
"Thus it is announced.
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
This person, [Name], seeks to receive full ordination from the preceptor, [Name]."
This man is twenty years of age; he possesses the three robes and the alms bowl, and has declared himself pure and free from all obstacles.
This person, [Name], requests the Saṃgha for the full ordination, with [Name] as preceptor.
The Sangha now confers full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as preceptor.
Those elders who consent to [Name] receiving full ordination with [Name] as preceptor remain silent; those who do not consent speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second is also spoken in this same manner as the first; the third is also spoken in this same manner as the first.
This concludes the third *karmavācanā*.
“‘So-and-so has completed the full ordination with So-and-so as preceptor.
Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Next, one should measure the shadow.”
"Listen, [Name]!

These four were spoken by the World-Honored One—the Knower, the Seer, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Fully Awakened One—for a bhikṣu who has thus gone forth and received full ordination; these are the four reliances."
Based on these four, one goes forth in the teaching of the self-arisen Dharma and receives full ordination as a bhikṣu.
These are few, easy to obtain, in accordance with the Dharma, unobstructed, foremost, untainted, and established from the beginning.
What are the four?
A bhikṣu wears rag-robes; he has gone forth under the teaching of the naturally existing Dharma, received full ordination, and become a bhikṣu.
[Name], are you able to wear rag-robes for as long as life lasts?
He replied, "I can. [The Buddha said:

"If there are long-term offerings—such as silk garments, white cotton cloth (*karpāsa*), plain cloth, light cloth, thread cloth, patched robes (*nāṃgaliya*), *kṣauma* cloth (fine soft cloth made from the fibers of the *kṣuma* plant), *kauśeya* cloth (garments woven from wild silkworm cocoons), *śāṇa* cloth (cloth woven from the bark of the *śāṇa* tree, which resembles hemp), *bhaṅga* cloth (woven from the fibers of the *bhaṅga* tree, the *guḍūcī* tree, or the *karpāsa* tree), camel hair wool, long-haired *karpāsa* cloth, or *sūkṣma-vastra* (fine cloth where wild silkworm cocoons serve as the woof and hemp or ramie serve as the warp)."

*Śāṇa* is like the hemp of this region. *Āvikā* cloth is woven from the thick wool of *karpāsa*. *Kambala* cloth is made by taking the fibers from the nests that insects build on *kambala* tree leaves and weaving them into garments. *Devadūṣya* cloth is made by taking the bark of the *devadūṣya* tree and weaving it into garments that have the color of donkey hair. *Kauśeya* cloth is made from *karpāsa* flowers; *kauśeya*, *kambala*, and *kambala*—these three types are interwoven to make the garment. *Pattrorṇa* cloth has *kauśeya* as the warp and *karpāsa* flowers as the woof. *Kāliṅga* cloth is woven from *karpāsa* flowers and dyed with wax to produce a variegated pattern. *Āpaṇaka* cloth is a mixture of *kṣauma* (hemp) and *karpāsa*.
"Regarding such robes as these—whether obtained from the Saṃgha or acquired by yourself—you should know the proper measure for receiving and keeping them.
Are you able to do so? He replied:
“Yes. “Listen, [Name]! A bhikṣu dwells under a tree;
he has gone forth from the household life into homelessness and received full ordination according to the teaching of the Dharma that is self-evident, becoming a bhikṣu.
"Venerable [Name], are you able to dwell beneath a tree for as long as life lasts?
He replies, "I am able."

"If one should long receive offerings—such as dwellings, grottoes, multi-storied pavilions, halls, and palaces; with eaves suspended like the shape of the moon, opening upward on all sides, with inner grottoes facing one another from the four directions; or having windows throughout, or having walkways or no walkways; or a thatched hut, or a leaf hut, or a grass house, or a leaf house, or a wooden chamber; or covered with grass, or covered with leaves, or covered with thorns, or covered with mats; or a clay grotto, or a stone grotto; or having a high foundation, or having no high foundation."
"There are such things as these, obtained from the Saṃgha or acquired by oneself; regarding these, you should know the proper measure for receiving and keeping them.
Are you able to do so? He replied:
“Yes. “Listen, [Name]! A bhikṣu lives by alms-gathering;
he has gone forth and received full ordination within the naturally arisen Dharma and Vinaya to become a bhikṣu.”
"Venerable so-and-so, are you able to sustain yourself by means of alms-seeking for as long as life lasts?
He replies, "I am able."

"If you receive abundant offerings—whether food or fruit, whether from regular allotments or special invitations, whether on the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day of the month, whether obtained in a communal gathering, from the Saṅgha, or acquired by yourself—you should know moderation in accepting these things."
"Can you do so? He replied, "I can."
“Listen, [Name]! A bhikṣu relies upon discarded medicines;
within this naturally established Dharma teaching, he has gone forth and received full ordination to become a bhikṣu.”
"Venerable [Name], are you able to rely on discarded medicine for your own use for as long as life lasts?
Can you do so? He replies:

"Yes. "If one should receive an abundance of offerings—whether medicinal roots, stems, leaves, flowers, or fruits; or ghee, oil, honey, or rock sugar; or medicines for the morning, medicines for the evening, or medicines for seven days, or lifelong medicines—whether obtained from the Sangha or acquired by oneself."
"You should know that you must receive [the precepts] in measured portions.
Are you able to do so? He replied:
“Yes. “Listen, [Name]!

These four are the points of falling away as spoken by the World-Honored One—the one who knows and sees, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—concerning those who have thus gone forth, received full ordination, and become bhikṣus.”

If a bhikṣu falls from this, he is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a renunciant, no longer a son of the Śākya; having lost the dharma of a bhikṣu, he has fallen away, been severed, turned back, degraded, and returned to the secular state, being unable to maintain the dharma of a śramaṇa.
Just as when a *tāla* tree is cut down, it no longer sprouts, grows, or turns green;

so too, a bhikṣu who falls from any one of these four dharmas is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer an ascetic, and no longer a son of the Śākya. He has lost the dharma of a bhikṣu and broken the dharma of a śramaṇa. Thus he is fallen, severed, turned back, degraded, and returned; he is unable to uphold the dharma of a śramaṇa.
What are the four?

O World-Honored One, Knower of the manifold, Seer, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, you have censured sexual desire as a cavern, sexual desire as a defiling stain; you have declared that sexual desire is ultimately a state of attachment, extreme attachment, and indulgent immersion—a cavern that is ultimately endless.

Such sensual desire is a dharma of emptiness, deception, and false ignorance; it deludes and misleads foolish people and is foul, filthy, and impure. It stands in opposition to, or is contrary to, that which is called the abandonment of desire, the state of being free from desire, tranquility, and ultimate cessation.
"You, [Name], from this day forward, you must not even look at women with a mind of attachment and craving, much less engage in sexual intercourse together with another person."

"O [Name]! The World-Honored One has already declared: if a bhikṣu, while training together with other bhikṣus and not having renounced the precepts, should—while his precepts are impaired—conceal his transgression and engage in unchaste conduct, the practice of sexual desire, even with an animal; because of this matter, he falls from the status of a bhikṣu. He is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer an ordained person, no longer a son of the Śākya. Having fallen from the status of a bhikṣu and broken the conduct of a śramaṇa, he has fallen, been severed, turned back, degraded, and returned; he is unable to maintain the dharma of a śramaṇa."
Just as when a *tāla* tree is cut down, it can no longer turn green, nor can it grow or increase in size;

even so, a bhikṣu who falls in this matter and at this point is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, and no longer a son of the Śākya. He has lost the dharma of a bhikṣu and destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa. He has fallen away, been severed, turned back, degraded, and retreated; he is unable to maintain the dharma of a śramaṇa.
From this day forward, you must not transgress; do not let this rule of falling away be violated.
Diligently apply mindfulness, guard it with continuous recollection, and be careful not to be negligent.
"If there is such a case or such a matter, you must not follow it. "Venerable sir!

The Blessed One—who possesses various forms of knowledge and vision, who knows and sees, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—has censured taking what is not given and praised the relinquishing of taking what is not given."

"You, [Name], from this day forward, you must not, with a mind of theft, take the property of others that has not been given—even so much as a grain of husk or a seed of hemp—let alone taking five *kārsāpaṇas* or more than five."

"Elder! The Blessed One has already declared: 'If a bhikkhu, whether in a village or in the wilderness, takes another's property that was not given, having conceived the intent to steal—that taking what is not given—may cause him to be seized by the king or his ministers, or to be beaten, bound, or banished.'"
He speaks these words:
"Ho there, man! You are a thief!
You are a fool! You are deluded! You are a robber!"

If a bhikṣu falls into such a state, he is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, and no longer a son of the Śākya; he has lost the dharma of a bhikṣu and broken the dharma of a śramaṇa. He has fallen away, been severed, turned back, degraded, and returned to the lay state; he is no longer able to uphold the dharma of a śramaṇa.
Just as when a *tāla* tree is cut down, it can no longer turn green, nor grow, nor expand;

so too, a bhikṣu who has fallen into this state is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, and no longer a son of the Śākya. Having lost the dharma of a bhikṣu and broken the dharma of a śramaṇa, he is then ruined, severed, turned back, fallen, and returned; he is unable to maintain the dharma of a śramaṇa.
From this day forward, you must not transgress; do not overstep these rules of falling (pācittiya).
Diligently apply mindfulness, guard it with continuous recollection, and be careful not to be negligent.
"If there is such a possibility or such a situation, you must not follow it.

"You, [Name], the World-Honored One—who possesses various kinds of knowledge and vision, who knows and sees, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—has censured the taking of life and has praised and extolled extensively the abandoning of the taking of life."

You, [Name], from this day forth, you should not intentionally or deliberately take the life of even insects such as mosquitoes, gadflies, or ants; how much less should you kill humans or human beings?

"Such-and-such a person, the World-Honored One has already declared: if a bhikṣu, having formed the intention and given it thought, kills a human being or one who is human-like—whether by taking up a knife himself, or by commanding another to kill, or by rejoicing in the killing, or by praising the killing, saying: 'Ho, man!'"
"What use have you for this sinful, painful, impure, and wretched life? Ho, man!
Death would be better for you than life!"
If one rejoices in the heart, or reflects upon it with thought, and by various causes and conditions encourages or praises death;

and if that person dies because of this matter, then the bhikṣu falls from this state: he is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, no longer a son of the Śākya; he has lost the dharma of a bhikṣu and broken the dharma of a śramaṇa. Thus he is ruined, severed, turned back, fallen, and returned; he is no longer able to maintain the dharma of a śramaṇa.
Just as when a *tāla* tree is cut down, it can no longer become green, nor grow, nor expand;

so too, a bhikṣu who falls into this state is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, and no longer a son of the Śākya. Having lost the dharma of a bhikṣu and broken the dharma of a śramaṇa, he has fallen away, been severed, turned back, descended, and retreated; he is no longer able to maintain the dharma of a śramaṇa.
From this day forward, you must not transgress; do not overstep this rule of downfall.
Diligently apply mindfulness, guard your continuous recollection, and be careful not to be negligent.
"If there is such a possibility or such a circumstance, you must not follow it.

"O [Name], the World-Honored One—who possesses various kinds of knowledge and vision, who knows and sees, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—reproaches falsehood and extensively praises and extols the abandonment of falsehood."

"You, [Name], from this day forward, you should not intentionally speak false words even in jest, much less falsely claim to possess superhuman states or super-saintly qualities and wisdom that do not exist, whether by asserting it as your own realization or your own vision, saying:
'I know this; I see this.'"

"Venerable sir, the Blessed One has already declared: 'If a bhikṣu, being ignorant and lacking knowledge, speaks of what he has not experienced; being without [such realization], he claims it exists; he speaks of a superhuman state (uttarimanussa-dhamma), claiming: "I have attained a supreme noble attainment," whether by realization or by vision, saying: "I know this, I see this."'"
What is known?
One knows suffering, one knows its origin, one knows its cessation, and one knows the path.
What is seen?
They see devas, see nāgas, see yakṣas, see asuras, see garuḍas, see gandharvas, see kiṃnaras, see mahoragas, see pretas, see bhūtas, and see kumbhāṇḍas down to the piśācas.
The devas also see me; the nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, pretas, kumbhāṇḍas, and even the pūtanās see me as well.
I shall also go to visit the devas, as well as the nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, pretas, kumbhāṇḍas, and even the piśācas.
The devas also come to me; nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, pretas, kumbhāṇḍas, and even the pāṃsupiśācas come to me as well.

I converse with the devas, exchanging greetings and engaging in discourse with them; I also converse with nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, pretas, kumbhāṇḍas, and even piśācas, exchanging greetings and engaging in discourse with them.

The devas also converse with me, exchanging greetings and engaging in discussion; likewise, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, pretas, kumbhāṇḍas, and even piśācas also converse with me, exchanging greetings and engaging in discussion.
"Whatever my companions have attained, I too have attained.

Such as the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self, the perception of repulsiveness in food, the perception of the lack of delight in all worlds, the perception of impurity, the perception of the livid, the perception of the worm-infested, the perception of the bloated and blood-stained, the perception of dismemberment, the perception of despondency, the perception of detachment, the perception of cessation, the perception of the skeleton, and the perception of contemplating emptiness—whatever they have attained, I too have attained."

Through loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, I have attained the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas; the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; as well as the power of the divine foot, the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and the exhaustion of outflows—I am an Arhat who has attained the eight liberations of dhyāna.

If a bhikṣu falls into this state, he is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, and no longer a son of the Śākya; he has lost the dharma of a bhikṣu and shattered the dharma of a śramaṇa. He has fallen away, been severed, turned back, degraded, and returned to the secular state; he is no longer able to uphold the dharma of a śramaṇa.
Just as when a tala tree is cut down, it can no longer turn green, grow, or expand;

so too, a bhikṣu who has fallen into this state is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, and no longer a son of the Śākya. Having lost the dharma of a bhikṣu and broken the dharma of a śramaṇa, he has fallen away, been severed, turned back, fallen, and retreated; he is no longer able to uphold the dharma of a śramaṇa.
From this day forward, you must not violate this; do not transgress this rule of falling away (*pācittiya*).
Diligently apply mindfulness, guard it with constant attention, and be careful not to be negligent.
“If there is such a possibility or such a circumstance, you must not follow it.

“These four, O Bhikṣu who has gone forth and received full ordination under the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—the one who knows and sees—have been taught as the duties of a śramaṇa by the Tathāgata for the sake of fulfilling the state of a śramaṇa.”
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves for as long as life lasts.
What are these four?
You, [Name], when reviled, should not revile in return; this is the first dharma of a śramaṇa.
In this regard, you should train yourself for as long as life lasts:
not to retaliate with anger when one is met with anger; this is the second quality of a śramaṇa.
In this regard, you should train yourself for as long as life lasts.
Not retaliating against those who revile you—this is the third dharma of a śramaṇa.
You should practice this throughout your entire life.
Not retaliating against those who strike you—this is the fourth dharma of a śramaṇa.
"You should practice and train in this for as long as you live.
You should practice and train in these four rules of training. "Listen, [Name]!
That which you have long desired— going forth in the self-arisen teaching, receiving full ordination, and becoming a bhikṣu— if a person goes forth,
they obtain a legitimate upādhyāya, obtain a legitimate ācārya, and obtain a legitimate saṃgha that performs the unshakeable *jñapti-caturtha-karman* in accordance with the Dharma.

If a bhikṣu has gone forth and received full ordination for a hundred years, he should train as one who is training; and one who has gone forth and received full ordination on this very day [should train] in the same way.

The precepts to be trained in are identical and without difference between one who has gone forth for a hundred years and one who has gone forth today. They share the same precepts, the same training, and the same recitation of the Prātimokṣa.
"In this regard, you should draw near to him and not distance yourself from him.
From this day forward, for as long as life lasts, you should provide service and support to your preceptor.
If your preceptor falls ill, you must also attend to him."
From the time your preceptor’s life comes to an end, whether he is rising or reclining, you should regard him as a father, and the preceptor should likewise regard you as a son.
From this day forward, you should give rise to reverence and joy toward your fellow students; you should follow with caution and respect those who are seniors and juniors.

From this day forward, you should all learn from them through reading, reciting, upholding, and explaining. You should skillfully study and discern the aggregates (*skandha*), skillfully discern the elements (*dhātu*), skillfully discern the sense bases (*āyatana*), and skillfully discern the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); you should lay down the heavy burden.

"Because you have not yet attained what has not been attained, because you have not yet understood what has not been understood, and because you have not yet realized what has not been realized, you should train yourself;
you should exhaust all outflows. 'Listen, [Name]!'"
I shall now, within this assembly of the Sangha, proclaim for you these most excellent precepts.
As for the others, your upādhyāya and ācārya shall explain them to you separately;
furthermore, you shall converse and discourse with your fellow student bhikṣus, mutually praising one another with joy.
Your preceptors and instructors shall also explain it to you;
furthermore, when the precepts are recited every half-month, you shall hear them therein as well.
"You have already received full ordination; within this Dharma of supreme wisdom, you should cultivate close association with it.

To encounter this is extremely rare: for one of upright character to go forth, and for one who is pure to receive the precepts. What has been spoken is the true name, known through the excellent knowledge and vision of the Perfectly Awakened One."
"You, [Name], have already received full ordination.
You must guard it well; be careful not to be negligent.
Thus did the World-Honored One speak to the bhikṣus regarding the reception of full ordination.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had been ordained for only one year, yet he conferred the full ordination upon others.
There is a specific causal origin (*nidāna*) for this, which should be treated as a fundamental narrative (*vṛttaka*).
Likewise, [there were those] with two years, four years, or five years of seniority who conferred the full ordination upon others.
The bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One who has completed only one year of seniority may not allow others to go forth from home and receive full ordination."
Even those with nine years of seniority may not ordain others as monks or grant them full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Should one ordain another as a monk and grant them full ordination, one incurs the *sthūlātyaya* offense.
"However, at ten *vassa*, one may ordain others as renunciants and confer upon them the full precepts (*upasampadā*).
At that time, the Bhikṣus [understood] that the World-Honored One had permitted those with ten years of seniority to ordain others as renunciants and confer upon them the full precepts.
At that time, a bhikṣu who has completed ten years since his full ordination may ordain others, allowing them to leave the household life and receive the full precepts.

Yet, if such a bhikṣu of ten years' standing is extremely foolish and dull-witted, lacking clarity and skillful means, and if he himself is not yet disciplined while wishing to discipline others—this is impossible.
The Buddha said:
"One who has not yet attained clear understanding after ten years of ordination shall not ordain others for renunciation or grant them the full precepts (*upasampadā*).
If one does so ordain others for renunciation and grant them the full precepts, one incurs the *sthūlātyaya* offense."
"However, one who has ten years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*), possesses clear understanding, and is capable may allow others to go forth and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
In this way, one who practices according to the teaching attains *sātisāra*."
The Abhidharma Sūtra of the Buddha, Chapter on the Characteristics of Renunciation, Part Two.
